pages.text: The Black Sea slave trade moved people from Eastern Europe and the Caucasus to the Mediterranean and the Middle East. This trade lasted from ancient times until the nineteenth century. The Black Sea region was ideal for trading war captives because empires and major trade routes met there.
pages.caption: Mine workers in Greece were often slaves.

evidence.articleCaption: Mine workers in Greece were often slaves.

pages.text: In ancient times, Greek and Roman city ports sold enslaved people. They sent them east to Asia along the Silk Road and west to the Mediterranean world. Ancient Greek colonies traded people from the interior North of the Black Sea. Families sometimes sold their members, or people were captured in wars.

pages.text: During the Middle Ages, religious borders created informal slave zones. Christians and Muslims banned enslaving people of their own faith, but they approved of enslaving people with different faiths. The Byzantine Empire imported slaves from the Vikings and from other traders who brought captives to Black Sea ports.
pages.caption: Genoese Castle in Caffa, when Caffa was a major port of the Genoese slave trade.

evidence.articleCaption: Genoese Castle in Caffa, when Caffa was a major port of the Genoese slave trade.

pages.text: In the late Middle Ages, trading colonies from Venice and Genoa took control of the Northern Black Sea coasts. They bought captives and transported them as slaves to Italy, Spain, and the Ottoman Empire. Later, the Crimean Khanate became a major center for the international slave trade.
pages.caption: The battle of Wadi al-Khazandar, 1299, depicting Mongol archers and Mamluk cavalry. During that time many mamluk soldiers originated from the Balkan slave trade and the Black Sea slave trade.

evidence.articleCaption: The battle of Wadi al-Khazandar, 1299, depicting Mongol archers and Mamluk cavalry. During that time many mamluk soldiers originated from the Balkan slave trade and the Black Sea slave trade.

pages.text: The Crimean Khanate made a large income by abducting Eastern Europeans through slave raids. When Russia conquered Crimea in 1783, the Crimean slave trade ended. After that, the Circassian slave trade became independent, trafficking women from the Caucasus to the Muslim world until the twentieth century.

B1-B2.headline: History of the Black Sea Slave Trade

pages.text: The Black Sea slave trade trafficked people from Eastern Europe and the Caucasus to destinations in the Mediterranean and the Middle East. Operating from antiquity until the nineteenth century, this major trade network thrived because the Black Sea was surrounded by shifting imperial borders, conquests, and key routes like the Ancient Silk Road.
pages.caption: Mine workers in Greece were often slaves.

evidence.articleCaption: Mine workers in Greece were often slaves.

pages.text: In antiquity, people were sold through ancient Greek and Roman city ports along the Black Sea. Greek colonies engaged in trading captives from northern interior tribes, exporting them west to the Mediterranean or east along the Silk Road. This trade continued even after Greek cities became vassals of the Roman Empire within the Bosporan Kingdom.

pages.text: During the Middle Ages, informal slave zones formed along religious borders. While both Christians and Muslims banned enslaving co-religionists, they permitted the enslavement of outsiders. The Byzantine Empire imported slaves transported by Vikings via northern routes, while various traders shipped captives down to Byzantine ports and Constantinople.
pages.caption: Genoese Castle in Caffa, when Caffa was a major port of the Genoese slave trade.

pages.text: In the late Middle Ages, Genoese and Venetian trading colonies on the Northern Black Sea coast used unstable political and religious borders to acquire captives. They exported these slaves to Italy, Spain, and the Ottoman Empire. By the early modern period, the Crimean Khanate emerged as another major center of the international slave trade.

pages.text: The Crimean Khanate generated massive income by abducting Eastern Europeans through coordinated slave raids. Families of wealthy prisoners could pay a ransom to secure their release, which typically matched or doubled the normal market price. When Russian conquest ended the Crimean trade in 1783, the Circassian slave trade from the Caucasus became an independent route supplying women to the Muslim world until the twentieth century.

C1-C2.headline: Dynamics of the Black Sea Slave Trade

pages.text: Spanning from antiquity through the nineteenth century, the Black Sea slave trade systematically trafficked populations from Eastern Europe and the Caucasus toward markets in the Mediterranean and the Middle East. The geographic configuration of the Black Sea—historically defined by imperial peripheries, military conquests, and converging thoroughfares such as the Ancient Silk Road—rendered it exceptionally well-suited for a commerce centered on war captives.
pages.caption: Mine workers in Greece were often slaves.

evidence.articleCaption: Mine workers in Greece were often slaves.

pages.text: During antiquity, coastal Greek and Roman port cities functioned as conduits for this traffic, dispersing enslaved individuals eastward along the Silk Road and westward into the broader Mediterranean. Greek foundations established along the Black Sea littoral facilitated exchanges between interior northern tribes and external buyers, a dynamic that persisted seamlessly as these municipalities transitioned into Roman vassal states within the Bosporan Kingdom.

pages.text: Medieval operations were structured around religious demarcations that prohibited co-religionist enslavement while validating the subjugation of religious outsiders. Byzantine importation mechanisms relied heavily on northern routes utilized by Vikings and intermediary traders, channeling captives through Black Sea ports and Constantinople toward domestic consumption and Middle Eastern markets.
pages.caption: Genoese Castle in Caffa, when Caffa was a major port of the Genoese slave trade.

evidence.articleCaption: Genoese Castle in Caffa, when Caffa was a major port of the Genoese slave trade.

pages.text: The late medieval period witnessed maritime republics such as Venice and Genoa establishing Crimean colonies that exploited volatile political and religious borderlands. These merchant networks redirected enslaved populations toward Southern Europe and the Islamic world. Subsequently, the early modern Crimean Khanate institutionalized large-scale raiding as a primary fiscal pillar, utilizing Caffa as the central hub where captives were processed and transferred to Ottoman merchants.

evidence.articleCaption: The battle of Wadi al-Khazandar, 1299, depicting Mongol archers and Mamluk cavalry. During that time many mamluk soldiers originated from the Balkan slave trade and the Black Sea slave trade.

pages.text: While affluent captives could frequently secure liberation through structured ransom payments equivalent to or exceeding standard market valuations, mass subjugation remained economically foundational. Following the definitive termination of Crimean operations via Russian conquest in 1783, the regional paradigm shifted toward the Circassian trade, sustaining a specialized luxury trafficking of women from the Caucasus through Anatolia and Constantinople well into the twentieth century.
